corrosive

/kuh-ROH-siv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Corrosive means tending to erode, eat away, or destroy something gradually through chemical action.

Road salt is corrosive: after a few winters it eats shining car panels down to lacework rust.

Example

When Maya finally opened the flashlight that had sat in the drawer for years, she found the batteries crusted with white powder. The leaked acid had eaten through the metal contacts, leaving them pitted and green. Her father showed her the ruined spring, chewed thin as wire. 'That's what a corrosive chemical does,' he said. 'Not all at once — it gnaws.'

The battery acid slowly ate through the metal contacts and spring — the gradual chemical gnawing that corrosive describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

acidic: Acidic means having the chemistry of an acid, which is one common way of eating away at a surface. Corrosive is broader: it covers anything — acid, road salt, leaked battery fluid — that destroys its target gradually through chemical action. Every acidic spill is corrosive, but plenty of corrosive agents are not acids at all.

erosive: Erosive describes gradual wearing away, and it is the word for wind, water, and ice slowly sculpting rock over years. Corrosive damage is also gradual, but it works by chemical attack and implies harm — salt eating a car panel, acid pitting steel. A river is erosive; a leaking battery is corrosive.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

protective: shielding something from damage

harmless: causing no damage at all

Where it sits · from mechanical wear to fierce chemical attack — abrasive → corrosive → caustic

abrasive vs. corrosive: Abrasive materials wear surfaces down by friction, while corrosive ones destroy through chemical action.

caustic vs. corrosive: Caustic substances are corrosive at their fiercest — able to burn or dissolve living tissue on contact.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — cor-

Prefix — cor-: thoroughly (a form of Latin com-)

Root — ros-

Root — ros-: to gnaw (Latin rodere)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Corrosive builds on Latin cor- (an intensive form of com-, 'thoroughly') plus rodere, 'to gnaw': 'tending to gnaw through.' The same gnawing root names the rodents — nature's tireless gnawers — and appears in erode. Corridor merely shares a few letters; its root is Latin currere, 'to run.'

Use the root in a new word: rodent

Use the root in a new word: rodent: Rodents get their name from Latin rodere, 'to gnaw' — the same gnawing root at the heart of corrosive.

Word Choice

technical; also figurative

Corrosive harm always eats away at one target, whether literally (acid on metal) or figuratively (sarcasm slowly eating away at trust); pernicious harm, another word in this unit, spreads more broadly and stealthily through a whole system rather than gnawing at a single thing.
